lead: A single-mode fiber actually carries two modes: the same field pattern polarized along two perpendicular axes. In a perfectly round, stress-free fiber they travel at the same speed. Real fiber is slightly elliptical and stressed, so the two polarizations see slightly different indices and drift apart in time. That delay is polarization mode dispersion (PMD). Along a cable the axes twist at random, so the mean delay grows as the square root of length. Only a few syllabi list PMD, but it limits links at 10 Gbit/s and above.

blocks.text: Drawing and cabling leave the core slightly non-circular and add stress that is not the same in all directions. The index is then n<sub>x</sub> along one transverse axis and n<sub>y</sub> along the other. Their difference is the birefringence, written here δn = |n<sub>x</sub> − n<sub>y</sub>| (the letter B is kept for the bit rate). The two axes are the principal axes.
Birefringence makes the polarization state change along the fiber. The state repeats after one beat length:

blocks.where: L<sub>B</sub> is the beat length in m; λ is the wavelength in m; δn is the birefringence (a pure number).

blocks.text: In a short piece of fiber whose axes stay fixed, the delay between the two polarizations, the differential group delay (DGD), grows in proportion to length: Δτ ≈ L δn/c when the dispersion of δn is ignored. With δn = 5 × 10⁻⁷ at 1550 nm the beat length is 3.1 m and the DGD is 1.67 ps per kilometre. Polarization-maintaining fiber does the opposite on purpose: stress rods give δn ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁴, a 5 mm beat length, and the two axes stay locked.

sections.h3: Random axes give a square-root law

blocks.text: In an installed cable the principal axes do not stay fixed. Bends, twists and temperature rotate them every few tens of metres, so power swaps between the two polarizations again and again. Each section adds a small delay that may add to or subtract from the total, like the steps of a random walk. The mean DGD therefore grows as √L:

blocks.where: ⟨Δτ⟩ is the mean DGD in ps; D<sub>PMD</sub> is the PMD coefficient in ps/√km; L is the length in km.

blocks.text: Modern fiber has D<sub>PMD</sub> of about 0.02 to 0.1 ps/√km; cable laid before the late 1990s can exceed 0.5 ps/√km. The DGD at any moment is random and follows a Maxwellian distribution. The chance that it exceeds twice the mean is 1.7 %, and three times the mean only 4.2 × 10⁻⁵, but over years of service a link does reach those values for minutes at a time.
A common design rule for direct-detection links keeps the mean DGD below a tenth of the bit period:

blocks.where: both sides in ps; T<sub>b</sub> = 1/B is the bit period, 100 ps at 10 Gbit/s and 25 ps at 40 Gbit/s.

blocks.text: PMD differs from chromatic dispersion in three ways: it scales as √L, not L; it does not depend on the source spectral width; and it changes with time, so it cannot be cancelled by a fixed spool of fiber.

examples.question: A 400 km link uses fiber with D<sub>PMD</sub> = 0.1 ps/√km. (a) Find the mean DGD. (b) Check it against the 0.1 T<sub>b</sub> rule at 10 Gbit/s and at 40 Gbit/s. (c) How often does the DGD exceed the 40 Gbit/s limit by the three-times-mean tail?
steps: (b) At 10 Gbit/s: T<sub>b</sub> = 100 ps, limit 10 ps. The mean of 2 ps passes easily.
At 40 Gbit/s: T<sub>b</sub> = 25 ps, limit 2.5 ps. The mean of 2 ps passes, with only 0.5 ps to spare.
(c) Three times the mean is 6 ps, above the 2.5 ps limit. The Maxwellian chance of exceeding 3⟨Δτ⟩ is 4.2 × 10⁻⁵, about 22 minutes a year (4.2 × 10⁻⁵ × 525 600 min).
Even 2⟨Δτ⟩ = 4 ps breaks the limit, with a chance of 1.7 %, so at 40 Gbit/s this link has frequent PMD outages.
examples.answer: Mean DGD 2 ps: safe at 10 Gbit/s; at 40 Gbit/s the mean passes but the random excursions above 2.5 ps make the link unreliable without PMD compensation.

examples.question: A 40 Gbit/s link must keep ⟨Δτ⟩ ≤ 2.5 ps. Find the longest link on fiber with D<sub>PMD</sub> = 0.1 ps/√km and on older fiber with 0.5 ps/√km.
steps: The coefficient is five times larger, and the reach is 5² = 25 times shorter.
examples.answer: 625 km on the new fiber but only 25 km on the old one, which is why old cable is measured for PMD before an upgrade.

traps: Using Δτ proportional to L for a cable. Linear growth holds only for a short piece with fixed axes; a real cable gives D<sub>PMD</sub>√L.
Writing D<sub>PMD</sub> in ps/km. Its unit is ps/√km.
Comparing the mean DGD with the whole bit period. The usual rule uses one tenth of it.
Treating the mean as the worst case. The DGD is random and its Maxwellian tail exceeds twice the mean 1.7 % of the time.
Thinking a narrower laser reduces PMD. PMD does not depend on the spectral width; chromatic dispersion does.

quiz.q: What is birefringence in a single-mode fiber?
quiz.a: The index difference δn = |n<sub>x</sub> − n<sub>y</sub>| between the two principal polarization axes, caused by core ellipticity and stress.

quiz.q: Why does the mean DGD of a cable grow as √L and not as L?
quiz.a: The principal axes rotate at random along the cable, so the delays of short sections add like a random walk: the variance grows as L, the mean as √L.

quiz.q: Find the beat length at 1310 nm of a fiber with δn = 2 × 10⁻⁶.
A fiber has D<sub>PMD</sub> = 0.2 ps/√km. Find the mean DGD over 900 km.
At 10 Gbit/s a link has a mean DGD of 4 ps. Check the 0.1 T<sub>b</sub> rule and the three-times-mean tail.
quiz.a: Limit 10 ps: the mean passes. The tail 3 × 4 = 12 ps exceeds 10 ps, a chance of about 4 × 10⁻⁵, so rare outages are possible.

quiz.q: Why is PMD more serious at 40 Gbit/s than at 10 Gbit/s on the same fiber?
quiz.a: The bit period falls from 100 ps to 25 ps, so the limit falls from 10 ps to 2.5 ps while the DGD stays the same.

quiz.q: A link passes the mean-DGD rule but shows bursts of errors lasting minutes. Give a PMD reason.
quiz.a: The instantaneous DGD drifts with temperature and handling; a Maxwellian excursion to two or three times the mean can exceed the limit for a while.

beyond: Coherent receivers track the polarization state continuously and undo PMD in signal processing, so 100 Gbit/s and faster channels tolerate tens of picoseconds of mean DGD. ITU-T G.652.D cable specifies a link design value of at most 0.2 ps/√km. Field testers measure PMD by the interferometric or fixed-analyser methods before an old route is upgraded. Search for “PMD link design value”, “Maxwellian DGD distribution” and “PMD compensation coherent DSP”.

figure.caption: The mean DGD grows as √L. On fiber with 0.1 ps/√km it is 2.0 ps at 400 km and reaches the 2.5 ps limit for 40 Gbit/s at 625 km; on old fiber with 0.5 ps/√km the same limit is reached after only 25 km.

spec.aria: Graph of mean differential group delay against length up to 900 kilometres: a square-root curve for 0.1 picoseconds per root kilometre passing 2.0 picoseconds at 400 km and 2.5 at 625 km, a steep curve for 0.5 reaching 2.5 at 25 km, and a dashed limit line at 2.5 picoseconds.
